title: Do Not Mix What God Separated

memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "'Keep my decrees. Do not mate different kinds of animals. Do not plant your field with two kinds of seed. Do not wear clothing woven of two kinds of material.'" - Lev 19:19 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Three unusual commands, and Scripture does not explain them. We should admit that honestly rather than inventing a reason.

What we can see is the pattern. God separates things. He did it at creation — light from darkness, waters from land, each plant and creature according to its kind (Gen 1:4-25). These laws seem to have taught Israel that same lesson through the ordinary business of farming and getting dressed. Every field and every garment quietly said: your God is a God who distinguishes.

We should be careful here. This is not a command about racial or cultural separation, and it has been badly misused that way. Scripture explicitly celebrates the foreigner joining Israel — this very chapter commands loving the foreigner as yourself, only fourteen verses later.

Nor do these particular rules bind us. Believers today are not under the ceremonial law, and Paul warned against those who make rules about food and clothing into tests of spirituality (Col 2:16-23).

But the principle behind them still stands. God's people are called to be distinct — not by our fabric, but by our lives. Come out from them and be separate (2 Cor 6:17). Not separate from people. Separate from the things that dishonour God.

What in your life still needs untangling?

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Are you comfortable admitting when Scripture does not explain itself?
2. Where have you mixed together things that should be kept distinct?
3. What makes a Christian genuinely distinct today?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, thank You that You are a God of order who makes distinctions. Show me where my life has become tangled with what dishonours You, and make me distinct in the ways that truly matter. Amen.
